research.summary: Memory and compute budgets of automotive cockpit/DMS SoC platforms, from public primary sources (accessed 2026-07-25). Qualcomm SA8155P (3rd-gen Snapdragon Cockpit): Qualcomm's product brief rates the ML subsystem at >10 TOPS under 7 W with a 4x16 LPDDR4X interface up to 68 GBps; the Thundercomm reference platform carries 8 GB LPDDR4X, while a documented production example (Li Auto L9) pairs two SA8155P chips with 24 GB RAM total (~12 GB per chip) — so 8-12 GB per SA8155P head unit is typical. Qualcomm SA8295P (4th-gen, 5 nm): NPU widely reported at 30 TOPS (8x the 8155); the Lantronix/Qualcomm QAM8295P development platform carries 16 GB of eight-channel LPDDR4X at 2133 MHz. TI Jacinto: TDA4VM offers 8 TOPS (INT8) with a single 32-bit LPDDR4-4266 interface, and TI's SK-TDA4VM edge-AI kit ships with just 4 GB LPDDR4 — representative of dedicated DMS/front-camera designs; TDA4VH-Q1 scales to 32 TOPS with four LPDDR4 interfaces. NVIDIA: DRIVE AGX Orin delivers up to 254 TOPS, with Orin modules shipping in 32 GB/64 GB 256-bit LPDDR5 (204.8 GB/s) configurations; DRIVE AGX Thor delivers >1,000 INT8 TOPS (2,000 FP4 TFLOPS) and its developer kit carries 64 GB LPDDR5X at 273 GB/s. On DMS allocation within shared SoCs: quantitative public data is scarce, but Cipia discloses that on Ambarella's CV28 a Euro-NCAP-compliant basic DMS uses 50% of Arm cores and only 10% of the AI engine (60%/35% for the advanced config), and Smart Eye advertises the 'smallest CPU footprint on the market' — supporting the assumption that a DMS function is budgeted only a small fraction (roughly single-digit TOPS and low single-digit GB of RAM) of a cockpit SoC that it shares with IVI/cluster workloads. Implication for the feasibility study: SA8155P-class head units (8-12 GB shared RAM, ~10 TOPS NPU) leave little headroom for a resident 2B-7B VLM; SA8295P-class (16 GB+, 30 TOPS) is marginal but plausible for a quantized 2-3B model; Orin/Thor-class (32-64 GB, 254-1,000+ TOPS) has ample headroom.

research.summary: Transformer/LLM/VLM support on automotive-grade NPUs is real but highly uneven as of July 2026. TI TIDL: transformer support began with Processor SDK 9.1 (tag 09_01_00_05, Jan 2024) covering ViT/DeiT via MatMul, LayerNorm and Softmax with severe initial limits (8-bit-only softmax, ~30x perf gap); the current 11.x line removes most functional limits and validates DeiT, Swin, DETR and Segformer, but only vision transformers via ONNX are documented — no LLM/VLM decoder enablement. Qualcomm: the strongest LLM story — AI Hub's automotive catalog (SA7255P/SA8255P/SA8295P/SA8650P/SA8775P) includes Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct in w4/w8 quantization, and the Snapdragon Ride whitepaper claims the NPU excels at multi-layer transformer networks with large VLMs hosted on the Ride Elite tier; the Cerence CaLLM Edge SLM (Phi-3-based, 3.8B params, 4k context, 4-bit) is a shipping-oriented automotive head-unit LLM proof point. Ambarella is the most aggressive public demonstrator: N1 (CV3-HD-derived) runs 1-34B multi-modal LLMs (Llama2-13B at up to 25 tok/s under 50 W, Jan 2024), N1-655 runs Phi/Gemma/LLaVA-OneVision/Llama at 20 W (Jan 2025), and Ambarella showed an LLM describing automotive scenes running on the automotive CV3-AD at CES 2025. NXP: eIQ GenAI Flow (Nov 2024) brings LLM+RAG pipelines to i.MX 95 with Neutron-NPU-accelerated LLM inference on i.MX 95 B0, but demonstrated models are small (danube-500M int8/int4); nothing public found for S32. Renesas: R-Car V4H (34 TOPS CNN accelerator) has no public transformer support claim; explicit generative AI/LLM claims appear only with Gen 5 R-Car X5H (up to 400 TOPS, sampling 2025, LLM-enabled AI cockpit claims Dec 2025). Implication for 2B-7B VLM in-cabin work: Qualcomm and Ambarella have public evidence at the required model scale; TI supports only vision-transformer backbones (useful for the vision encoder, not the LM decoder); NXP is demonstrated only at sub-1B scale; Renesas capability arrives with Gen 5.

claims.topic: Euro NCAP distraction detection - long distraction
claims.claim: Euro NCAP's Safe Driving / Driver Engagement protocol (v1.1, October 2025, implementation January 2026) defines a Long Distraction as a single driver gaze away from the forward road lasting between 3 and 4 seconds, which in verification must be preceded by a 4-second on-road gaze; detection is assessed separately for Owl (head) and Lizard (eye) movement types.
claims.quote: A long distraction is defined as a single long duration driver gaze away from the forward road between 3 and 4 seconds. During the verification, it shall be ensured that the distraction is preceded by a four second on-road gaze.
claims.source_title: Euro NCAP Safe Driving – Driver Engagement Protocol, Version 1.1, October 2025 (Section 1.2.1)

claims.topic: Euro NCAP distraction detection - short distraction (VATS)
claims.claim: Euro NCAP defines Short Distraction (Visual Attention Time Sharing, VATS) as glances away from the forward road view accumulating to 10 seconds within a 30-second time period; alternative detection strategies are also eligible for points.
claims.quote: It is defined as a driver who glances away from the forward road view for a cumulative 10 seconds within a 30 second time period. Alternative detection strategies are also eligible for points.
claims.source_title: Euro NCAP Safe Driving – Driver Engagement Protocol, Version 1.1, October 2025 (Section 1.2.2)

claims.topic: Euro NCAP microsleep and sleep detection
claims.claim: Euro NCAP defines a microsleep event as a short-duration eye closure of 1-2 seconds, and classifies a driver as asleep when displaying a continued eye closure of >=3 seconds; each is worth 2 points in the 25-point Driver Monitoring assessment.
claims.quote: A driver is considered to be undergoing a microsleep event when displaying a short duration eye closure (1-2 seconds). [...] A driver is deemed asleep when displaying a continued eye closure ≥3 seconds.
claims.source_title: Euro NCAP Safe Driving – Driver Engagement Protocol, Version 1.1, October 2025 (Sections 1.3.3, 1.3.4)

claims.topic: Euro NCAP unresponsive driver detection
claims.claim: Euro NCAP allows classifying a driver as unresponsive when gaze does not return to the forward road view within 3 seconds after a distraction warning, or when the eyes have been closed for >=6 seconds; the Emergency Function intervention must start no later than 5 seconds after the distinct warning phase begins.
claims.quote: A driver may be classified as unresponsive when their gaze does not return to the forward road view within 3 seconds after a distraction warning being issued or when the eyes have been closed for ≥ 6 seconds.
claims.source_title: Euro NCAP Safe Driving – Driver Engagement Protocol, Version 1.1, October 2025 (Sections 1.3.5, 1.4.3.3)

claims.topic: Euro NCAP drowsiness detection threshold
claims.claim: For drowsiness points, Euro NCAP requires detection of a driver reaching Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) level >7 at the latest (or an equivalent metric), with the system functional from 50 km/h.
claims.quote: Systems capable of detecting a driver reaching a KSS level >7 at the latest, or an equivalent metric appropriate to assess risky levels of drowsiness are eligible to score points. The system shall be functional from 50 km/h.
claims.source_title: Euro NCAP Safe Driving – Driver Engagement Protocol, Version 1.1, October 2025 (Section 1.3.2)

claims.topic: Euro NCAP real-time response / latency requirements
claims.claim: Euro NCAP requires a visual plus haptic/audible warning to be issued immediately after a driver is classified as distracted at >=20 km/h; coupled FCW/AEB triggering time must differ by at least 200 ms between distracted and attentive drivers, and Forward Support Sensitivity intervention must be activated within <=1 second of any continuous gaze away from the forward road view.
claims.quote: FCW and/or AEB systems shall be coupled to the driver state so that the triggering time differs at least 200ms between a distracted and/or impaired driver and an attentive driver [...] the intervention strategy shall be activated ≤ 1 second of any continuous gaze away from forward road view
claims.source_title: Euro NCAP Safe Driving – Driver Engagement Protocol, Version 1.1, October 2025 (Sections 1.4.1, 1.4.3.1)

claims.topic: Euro NCAP DSM robustness envelope (noise variables)
claims.claim: To score DSM points, Euro NCAP requires functional performance across lighting from daytime 100,000 lux to night-time 1 lux, drivers aged 16-80, Fitzpatrick skin types 1-6, eyelid apertures from 6.0 mm up to 12.0 mm, and clear sunglasses with >70% transmittance (at the camera's operating wavelength); the DSM must start measuring driver state within 1 minute of driving at >=10 km/h.
claims.quote: Lighting | Daytime (100,000 lux) – night-time (1 lux) | Functional [...] Eye lid aperture | From 6.0mm up to 12.0mm | Functional
claims.source_title: Euro NCAP Safe Driving – Driver Engagement Protocol, Version 1.1, October 2025 (Section 1.1.1)

claims.topic: EU GSR - DDAW drowsiness warning requirements (Regulation (EU) 2021/1341)
claims.claim: Under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1341 (supplementing GSR 2019/2144), the DDAW system must warn the driver at a drowsiness level equivalent to or above 8 on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, must be automatically activated above 70 km/h, and must operate normally within 65 km/h to 130 km/h (or the vehicle's maximum allowed speed, whichever is lower).
claims.quote: The DDAW system shall provide a warning to the driver at a level of drowsiness which is equivalent to or above 8 on the reference sleepiness scale [...] The DDAW system shall be automatically activated above the speed of 70 km/h
claims.source_title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1341 of 23 April 2021 (DDAW), EUR-Lex

claims.topic: EU GSR - DDAW validation criteria and PERCLOS as alternative measure
claims.claim: DDAW validation under (EU) 2021/1341 is passed if average sensitivity is above 40% (or the lower bound of the 90% confidence interval of sensitivity results is above 20%), and manufacturers may validate using alternative direct driver-state measurements such as EEG or PERCLOS with documented equivalence to KSS thresholds.
claims.quote: the average sensitivity is above 40 % [...] If the alternative method directly monitors the participants' state, such as Electroencephalogram (EEG) or PERCLOS (percentage of eyelid closure)
claims.source_title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1341 of 23 April 2021 (DDAW), EUR-Lex

claims.topic: EU GSR - ADDW distraction warning time thresholds (Regulation (EU) 2023/2590)
claims.claim: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2590 requires the ADDW system to warn when the driver's gaze dwells in the defined 'Area 3' (distraction area) for a maximum of 3.5 seconds at vehicle speeds of 50 km/h or above, and 6 seconds at speeds of 20 km/h or above; non-nominal situations may extend these limits by an additional 1.5 seconds.
claims.quote: (a) vehicle's speed at 50 km/h or above; (b) the gaze of the driver in the Area 3 last for a maximum time of 3,5 seconds in the nominal situation. [...] (a) vehicle's speed at 20 km/h or above; (b) the gaze of the driver in the Area 3 last for a maximum time of 6 seconds in the nominal situation.
claims.source_title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2590 of 13 July 2023 (ADDW), Annex I Part 1, points 3.3.2.1-3.3.2.2, EUR-Lex

claims.topic: EU GSR - ADDW timing tolerances and test pass criteria
claims.claim: The ADDW regulation sets a minimum gaze-event time tolerance of 50 milliseconds to account for eye saccades, and in testing a measurement is a false negative if no distraction warning is emitted within 4 seconds (including a 0.5-second uncertainty buffer) for the 50 km/h / 3.5-second condition, or within 6.5 seconds for the 20 km/h / 6-second condition.
claims.quote: The allowed time tolerance for the events described shall be defined by the vehicle manufacturer, with a minimum time tolerance of 50 milliseconds (eye saccades). [...] no distraction warning is emitted within 4 seconds (which includes a 0,5 second uncertainty buffer)
claims.source_title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2590 of 13 July 2023 (ADDW), EUR-Lex

claims.topic: EU GSR - ADDW mandate timeline
claims.claim: The ADDW requirement under Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 applies from 7 July 2024 (per recital 6 of Regulation (EU) 2023/2590, which applies from the same date); ADDW systems have been required in all new EU vehicle types since July 2024 and become mandatory for all newly registered vehicles from July 2026.

research.summary: Real-time and functional requirements for DMS, from primary sources. (1) Euro NCAP Safe Driving / Driver Engagement Protocol v1.1 (Oct 2025, implementation Jan 2026; PDF read directly): Long Distraction = single 3-4 s off-road gaze (preceded by 4 s on-road); Short Distraction/VATS = cumulative 10 s off-road within a 30 s window; microsleep = 1-2 s eye closure; sleep = continued eye closure >=3 s; unresponsive = no gaze return within 3 s after a warning or eyes closed >=6 s; drowsiness = KSS >7 detection, functional from 50 km/h. Latency-critical items: warning 'immediately' after classification at >=20 km/h, FCW/AEB trigger-time differential >=200 ms between distracted and attentive drivers, forward-support intervention activated <=1 s of continuous off-road gaze, Emergency Function <=5 s after distinct warning. Robustness envelope spans 1-100,000 lux, Fitzpatrick skin types 1-6, eyelid apertures 6-12 mm. (2) EU GSR 2019/2144 delegated acts: DDAW (EU 2021/1341) warns at KSS >=8, auto-activates above 70 km/h, operates 65-130 km/h, validation sensitivity >40% average, PERCLOS/EEG allowed as alternative validation measures; ADDW (EU 2023/2590, applies from 7 July 2024, all new registrations July 2026) warns when gaze dwells in the distraction area >3.5 s at >=50 km/h or >6 s at >=20 km/h, with a 50 ms minimum saccade time tolerance and a 4 s (incl. 0.5 s buffer) false-negative test window. (3) Production DMS cameras: 940 nm NIR active illumination is the industry norm (ams OSRAM), paired with global-shutter NIR sensors such as OMNIVISION OV2311 (1600x1300 at up to 60 fps). (4) PERCLOS (FHWA TechBrief FHWA-MCRT-98-006, 1998): proportion of time in a one-minute window that eyes are >=80% closed (P80; variants P70, EYEMEAS), found the most reliable/valid alertness measure. Implication for a 2B-7B VLM on edge SoC: eye-state/gaze channels need frame-level cadence (50 ms saccade tolerance and 1-2 s microsleep detection imply roughly 30-60 fps perception with sub-second end-to-end classification latency), while drowsiness scoring (KSS/PERCLOS) accumulates over minutes and tolerates slower model cadence.

research.summary: Published evidence on small VLMs (1-8B) at the edge is mixed but consistent. On NVIDIA's own Jetson Orin Nano 8GB benchmarks (JetPack 6.2 Super Mode, tokens/sec), 2B-class VLMs are marginal for interactive use — Qwen2 VL 2B: 2.8 to 4.4 tok/s, SmolVLM 2B: 8.1 to 12.9 tok/s — while 7B-class VLMs are effectively non-real-time on that tier (LLaVA 1.6 7B INT4: 0.412 to 0.57 tok/s). Purpose-built mobile VLMs do far better: MobileVLM (arXiv) reports 21.5 tok/s on a Snapdragon 888 CPU and 65.3 tok/s on a Jetson Orin GPU, and Qualcomm demonstrated a 7B+ LLaVA running on-device on a Snapdragon phone (no tok/s published). Memory: the official Qwen2-VL-7B-AWQ card shows a 7B VLM drops from 16.07 GB (BF16) to ~7.07-7.20 GB (INT4/AWQ) and 10.11 GB (INT8) at minimal context, and Hugging Face reports SmolVLM 2B needs 5.02 GB vs 13.70 GB for Qwen2-VL 2B unquantized — so 8GB-class automotive SoCs can hold an INT4 7B VLM but with little headroom, while 2B INT4 models fit comfortably. For automotive: LiteVLM (arXiv, NVIDIA DRIVE Thor) shows 2.5-3.2x end-to-end VLM latency reductions (FP8) are achievable on automotive silicon; in-cabin-specific literature (arXiv 2606.26922, 2606.02273) currently concludes large VLMs are unsuitable as always-on in-cabin monitors due to latency/reliability and that zero-shot VLMs miss fine-grained driver behaviors (ACCR 66 vs 76 fine-tuned), while non-VLM in-cabin systems already hit 40-60 ms/frame on Raspberry Pi 5/Coral-class hardware — suggesting a feasibility posture of small/distilled VLMs for episodic reasoning plus lightweight CNNs for always-on monitoring. Key sources: developer.nvidia.com Orin Nano Super blog, huggingface.co/blog/smolvlm, Qwen2-VL-7B-AWQ model card, arXiv 2312.16886, 2506.07416, 2606.26922, 2512.22298, 2606.02273, and Qualcomm's Feb 2024 AI Hub press release.

claims.quote: Cost-aware selective inference reduces unsafe false negatives from 17.37% under always-fast inference to approximately 5% across seeds while preserving deployment-level latency.

research.summary: Industry landscape for VLM/LLM-based in-cabin monitoring, from public sources accessed 2026-07-25. (1) Supplier/OEM announcements: the on-device trend is explicit — LG's AI Cabin Platform (Dec 2025) runs VLMs/LLMs/image-generation models fully on-device on Qualcomm Snapdragon Cockpit Elite with no external servers, analyzing driver state from interior/exterior cameras; Visteon+Qualcomm (Apr 2025) run quantized LLMs on the Hexagon NPU via QNN in a hybrid multimodal architecture that stays in-vehicle; Bosch (Dec 2025) sells an add-on cockpit box on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Orin with 150-200 TOPS for in-cabin VLMs plus NVIDIA Nemotron reasoning. Qualcomm's Cockpit Elite SoC itself targets a 12x NPU boost with up to 20 cameras for in-cabin monitoring. Contrast: Sony Honda's AFEELA Personal Agent is cloud-based (Azure OpenAI Service), with a VLM planned in the end-to-end driving model, and Smart Eye's generative-AI co-driver 'Sheila' (CES 2025 honoree) fuses DMS sensing with generative AI without disclosing execution location. (2) Academic results: fine-tuned CLIP variants match or beat CNN baselines on distraction datasets (VideoCLIP 98.44% on DMD; single-frame CLIP 83.15% on StateFarm vs ResNet18 82.68/MobileNet-v2 80.04), but zero-shot VLM accuracy is far below deployable levels (48-58%); fine-tuning on driver-activity description data lifts ACCR from 66 to 76 on Drive&Act. (3) Distillation/hybrid triggers: arXiv 2606.26922 quantifies why raw VLMs cannot be always-on monitors (8615.98 ms per sample vs 3.08 ms for an 11.39M-parameter student) and shows a cost-aware selective/trigger architecture cutting unsafe false negatives from 17.37% to ~5%. Net takeaway for the feasibility study: industry consensus is small quantized multimodal models on cockpit NPUs (or added Orin compute) for latency-critical functions, cloud LLMs only for conversational layers, and academia converging on distilled students with VLM-as-verifier trigger designs rather than continuous VLM inference.
